source.version: Journal version of record: Computers in Human Behavior: Artificial Humans 8 (2026) 100302; received 15 February 2026, revised 25 March 2026, accepted 25 March 2026, available online 30 March 2026 (p. 1)
source.title_on_document: Who performs better? Exploring the role of generative AI in creativity and brainstorming

supplement.where: No online supplement is referenced. The appendix (Fig. 1, Table 1, Table 2) is printed on p. 9 of this PDF. Data and preregistration: https://osf.io/h6ztr/ (p. 9, Data availability).
supplement.holds: Nothing outside this PDF beyond the OSF data and preregistration. All statistics (F tests, eta squared, p values, cell and marginal means and SDs) are in the main text (pp. 6-7) and Table 1 (p. 9).

paper_design_summary: 212 undergraduates at a large public Midwestern US university (University of Wisconsin-Madison IRB) did a 10-minute individual brainstorm of ideas to improve the university's SOAR orientation program, in a 2 x 2 between-subjects lab design: independent versus AI-assisted ideation (Microsoft Copilot) crossed with an anticipated human versus AI teammate for a later group session. Blind trained undergraduate coders rated each idea for originality, feasibility, and fun (1-5, averaged per participant); the authors also counted ideas (quantity) and distinct idea categories (flexibility).

studies.label: Lab experiment: 2 x 2 (ideation condition x anticipated teammate) brainstorming on the SOAR program

assignment.what_was_assigned: Ideation condition (independent vs. AI-assisted with Microsoft Copilot) crossed with anticipated teammate (human vs. AI). The paper states random assignment to the four conditions, but the teammate factor followed arrival: participants who arrived in pairs anticipated a human teammate, and those who arrived alone were assigned to the AI-teammate condition.
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of the four conditions (Independent/Anticipated human teammate = 69; AI-assisted/Anticipated human teammate = 68; Independent/Anticipated AI teammate = 37; AI-assisted/Anticipated AI teammate = 38).
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 4 Method; teammate assignment by arrival on p. 5, Section 4.2 Study design
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 9, Data availability (https://osf.io/h6ztr/); Hypotheses 1 and 2 stated as pre-registered on pp. 3-4; Hypotheses 3a and 3b stated as non-preregistered on p. 4

arms.name: Independent / anticipated human teammate (HHT)
arms.description: Brainstormed alone; told a future teammate would be a human partner (paired with another participant who arrived for the same session).

arms.name: AI-assisted / anticipated human teammate (AI-HHT)
arms.description: Brainstormed with Microsoft Copilot; told a future teammate would be a human partner.

arms.name: Independent / anticipated AI teammate (HAT)
arms.description: Brainstormed alone; told a future teammate would be an AI teammate (participants who arrived alone).

arms.name: AI-assisted / anticipated AI teammate (AI-HAT)
arms.description: Brainstormed with Microsoft Copilot; told a future teammate would be an AI teammate.

participants.exclusions: 224 participants were recruited. 10 were excluded for failing condition-check items (anticipated partner or AI assistance); 2 more were excluded (one facilitator error with the written handout, one language barrier). Final sample 212. The per-condition counts (69, 68, 37, 38) sum to 212, so they are post-exclusion counts; the paper does not give counts at assignment by condition. The analysis is not intention-to-treat.
participants.who: Undergraduate students (75.5% female; mean age 20.02, SD 1.67) receiving one extra course credit, with a $20 gift card for the top 25% of task performance
participants.country: United States (large public university in the Midwest; IRB of University of Wisconsin-Madison)
participants.quote: A total of 224 participants were recruited for this in-person lab experiment at a large public university in the Midwestern United States.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 4.1 Participants; IRB on p. 8, Exemption statement

ai_tool.name_model: Microsoft Co-pilot (Auto mode), university-licensed; underlying model not stated
ai_tool.how_used: Participants logged into individual university Copilot accounts and were told to treat it as an assisting tool, asking "what" and "how" questions or getting suggestions. They had to type out their own ideas and could not use AI responses verbatim (p. 5, Sections 4.2-4.3).

task.description: Generate ideas to improve or redesign the university's Student Orientation, Advising, and Registration (SOAR) program to make it more engaging and helpful for incoming students; ideas typed into a Word document.
task.duration: 10 minutes (extended from 8 minutes after a pilot)

outcomes.name: Originality of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Trained undergraduate coders, blind to condition, rated each idea for originality (novelty and uniqueness) on a 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent) scale; participant score = mean across their ideas. ICC .76 (period 1, four coders on ~16% of ideas) and .84 (period 2, two coders on ~20%). Analyzed with 2 x 2 ANOVA; Bonferroni-adjusted simple effects.

contrasts.reported: Main effect of ideation condition F(1, 208) = 16.78, eta^2 = .075, p < .001. Table 1: Independent M 2.99 (SD .47) vs AI-Assisted M 3.34 (SD .56). Interaction with teammate F(1, 208) = 7.61, eta^2 = .035, p = .006.
AI-assisted M = 3.49, SD = .59 vs independent M = 2.99, SD = .47; F(1, 135) = 29.94, eta^2 = .182; p < .001, 95% CI [.32, .68] (Bonferroni-adjusted simple effect)
AI-assisted M = 3.09, SD = .43 vs independent M = 2.99, SD = .48; F(1, 73) = .87, eta^2 = .012; p = .36

outcomes.name: Feasibility of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same blind undergraduate coders; feasibility (ease of implementation) on a 1-5 scale, averaged per participant. ICC .70 (period 1) and .78 (period 2).

contrasts.reported: Main effect of ideation condition F(1, 208) = 2.71, eta^2 = .013, p = .101. Table 1: Independent M 3.43 (SD .56) vs AI-Assisted M 3.37 (SD .70). Interaction F(1, 208) = 10.80, eta^2 = .049, p = .001.
AI-assisted M = 3.51, SD = .66 vs independent M = 3.37, SD = .59; F(1, 135) = 1.85, eta^2 = .014; p = .176

outcomes.name: Fun (enjoyability) of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Same blind undergraduate coders; fun (perceived enjoyability of the idea) on a 1-5 scale, averaged per participant. ICC .71 (period 1) and .75 (period 2). The paper treats fun as a third component of idea quality alongside originality and feasibility.

contrasts.reported: Main effect of ideation condition F(1, 208) = 4.23, eta^2 = .020, p = .041. Table 1: Independent M 3.18 (SD .56) vs AI-Assisted M 3.44 (SD .73). Interaction F(1, 208) = 9.58, eta^2 = .044, p = .002.
AI-assisted M = 3.01, SD = .59 vs independent M = 3.10, SD = .52; F(1, 73) = .50, eta^2 = .007; p = .48

outcomes.name: Quantity of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Total number of unique ideas typed by each participant in the Word document.

contrasts.reported: Main effect of ideation condition F(1, 208) = 4.14, eta^2 = .020, p = .043. Table 1: Independent M 13.24 (SD 5.8) vs AI-Assisted M 11.69 (SD 7.00). Interaction F(1, 208) = 1.53, eta^2 = .007, p = .217. No cell means reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, Section 5.2 Quantity of ideas; p. 9, Table 1

outcomes.name: Flexibility of ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct idea categories in each participant's list, using a 13-category scheme developed by the team; coders blind to condition coded by hand after calibrating on 15 participants. This is variety within one person's ideas, not similarity across people.

contrasts.reported: Main effect of ideation condition F(1, 208) = 5.05, eta^2 = .024, p = .026. Table 1: Independent M 6.66 (SD 1.95) vs AI-Assisted M 6.06 (SD 2.22). Interaction F(1, 208) = .65, eta^2 = .003, p = .421. No cell means reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Section 5.4 Flexibility of idea; p. 9, Table 1

eligibility.reason: The paper states random assignment of individuals to four conditions, including independent vs. Copilot-assisted ideation (p. 4); 212 undergraduates analyzed (106 AI-assisted, 106 independent); originality, feasibility, fun, quantity, and flexibility are scored on the ideas by blind coders. Caveat for review: the anticipated-teammate factor was set by arrival (pairs vs. alone, p. 5), not by randomization, so the AI-vs-independent contrast is best read pooled or within teammate cells; the paper does not describe how the AI factor itself was randomized.

one_line_finding: Copilot-assisted brainstorming raised rated originality (Table 1: 3.34 vs 2.99, F(1, 208) = 16.78, p < .001) and fun (3.44 vs 3.18, p = .041) but lowered idea quantity (11.69 vs 13.24, p = .043) and flexibility (6.06 vs 6.66, p = .026), with no main effect on feasibility (pp. 6-7, Table 1 p. 9).
open_questions: How was the ideation condition (AI vs. independent) randomized, given that the teammate factor followed arrival? The OSF preregistration (https://osf.io/h6ztr/) may say.
The study is 'nested within a larger project'; do other papers from that project analyze the same participants?
Which outcome, if any, does the OSF preregistration name as primary? The paper names none; Hypothesis 1 covers quantity, quality, and flexibility.
notes: The impression-management scale (self-report, 5 items, 7-point) is a manipulation check and is not listed as an outcome; AI assistance had no effect on it (F(1, 208) = .413, p = .521; p. 6, Section 5.1). Main effects of anticipated teammate (human vs. AI) are not listed as contrasts because that factor does not vary AI assistance and was not randomized: originality F(1, 208) = 7.47, p = .007; fun F(1, 208) = 20.07, p < .001; quantity, feasibility, and flexibility not significant (pp. 6-7). Table 1 reports marginal means by ideation condition without ns; the condition ns (106 each) come from the cell counts on p. 4. Data were collected over two semesters with two coding periods (p. 5). No diversity-across-people outcome is reported.
